rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The injunction is to hold fast to the Quran, which keeps one on the straight path.
rows.anchor: The injunction is to hold fast to the Quran (IK, JJ, Ṭ), which ensures that one remains upon a straight path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This contrasts the Prophet's revelation with idolaters who had no prior book to follow.
rows.anchor: , in contrast to the idolaters, who were not given a book beforehand to which they hold fast (v. 21).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' story offers a spiritual example reflecting aspects of the Prophet Muhammad's own challenges.
rows.anchor: Here the account of Moses provides a spiritual example, reflecting aspects of the Prophet Muhammad’s own challenges.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary directs readers to fuller and shorter Quranic accounts of Moses' mission.
rows.anchor: For more detailed accounts of Moses’ mission, see 7:103–55; 10:75–93; 20:9–97; 26:10–66; 28:3–46.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's circle mocked Moses' signs as the Makkan idolaters mocked Muhammad's signs; Pharaoh, Hāmān, and Korah called Moses a lying sorcerer.
rows.anchor: they laughed at them in the same way that the Makkan idolaters mocked the signs with which the Prophet was sent (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Each sign Moses brought exceeded the sign immediately before it.
rows.anchor: Each of the signs that Moses brought was greater than the sign immediately before it (JJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, JJ
rows.claim: God punished Pharaoh's people for rejecting the signs in hope that they would repent and abandon disbelief.
rows.anchor: For their rejection of the signs, God punished them in the hope that they would repent (Ṭ) and recant their disbelief (JJ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh and his notables promised to believe and release the Children of Israel if Moses lifted the torment.
rows.anchor: A similar verse is 7:134, in which Pharaoh and the notables continue the address to Moses, saying

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Calling Moses a sorcerer was not an insult; by their worldview it may have honored him because they did not condemn sorcery.
rows.anchor: According to their worldview, this might in fact have been a way of honoring him (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They recognized Moses' evidentiary miracles, yet hardened disbelief made the miracles ineffective for them.
rows.anchor: but the miracles themselves had no ultimate effect on them, because they were hardened disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic miracles mainly elicit or encourage belief among people already disposed toward it, as with Moses' believing sorcerers.
rows.anchor: The primary function of prophetic miracles seems to be to elicit and encourage belief among those who are already somehow disposed to it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miracles distinguish good but misguided disbelievers from those, like Pharaoh, whose hearts are hardened against every prophetic sign or message.
rows.anchor: serve to distinguish the inherently good, but merely misguided, members of a disbelieving community from those, like Pharaoh, whose hearts were so thoroughly hardened

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs cannot convince those unwilling to believe a prophet's message.
rows.anchor: Regarding the inability of signs to convince those unwilling to believe in a prophet’s message

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses indicates that God's Words, rather than apparent supernatural feats, ultimately separate truth from falsehood and illusion.
rows.anchor: it is God’s Words (rather than apparent supernatural feats) that ultimately separate truth from falsehood and illusion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Moses' supplications lifted the punishment, Pharaoh's people returned to disbelief as soon as they felt safe.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh and his notables return to their inveterate disbelief as soon as they feel safe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People often call on God in need, then neglect Him once safe or at ease.
rows.anchor: human beings will often invoke God when they are in need and then neglect God when they are safe or at ease

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's claim about the streams displays haughtiness: from the Quranic perspective, God alone makes water flow.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh’s invocation of the streams running beneath his feet as a sign of his sovereignty demonstrates both his haughtiness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh is ignorant of how God may grant respite and remove worldly blessings at any moment.
rows.anchor: and his ignorance, since the Quran warns that God grants respite for a while, but can remove such blessings at any moment

rows.speaker: IK, JJ
rows.claim: Some commentators explain Pharaoh's charge about Moses' unclear speech as a lisp caused by a hot coal accidentally put in Moses' mouth as a child.
rows.anchor: to a lisp said to have resulted from a hot coal that was accidentally placed in his mouth when he was a child (IK, JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some accounts say Pharaoh lied because Moses' speech impediment had been removed after he asked God to untie his tongue.
rows.anchor: Thou hast been granted thy request, O Moses! (20:36; IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Pharaoh's words may assess the message Moses brought as difficult to understand.
rows.anchor: Alternately, it could be understood as Pharaoh’s assessment of the message that Moses brought.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh repeats the Makkan objection that a messenger should be wealthy or accompanied by an angel, as in objections to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Here Pharaoh exhibits the same misunderstandings expressed by the Makkan idolaters in the first half of the sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran answers that sending an angel would settle the matter and leave the disbelievers no respite.
rows.anchor: Had We sent down an angel, then the matter would be decreed, and they would be granted no respite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also says an angel would have been sent as messenger if angels walked the earth.
rows.anchor: Were there angels walking about upon the earth in peace, then We would have sent down upon them an angel from Heaven as a messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran gives many other examples of disbelievers objecting to prophets in this way.
rows.anchor: For the disbelievers’ various expressions of this objection to the prophets, see

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about inciting people to make light may instead mean that Pharaoh moved them to submit or to be foolish.
rows.anchor: Then he incited his people to make light could also mean that he moved them to submit or to be foolish.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran recounts Pharaoh and his army drowning in several other passages.
rows.anchor: This is one of several references in the Quran to the drowning of Pharaoh and his army

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet recited this verse after teaching that a sinful person receiving what he wants may be enticed toward destruction.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have recited this verse after saying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salaf, rendered as “a bygone people,” can here mean “a precedent.”
rows.anchor: A bygone people renders salaf, which in this context could also be understood as “a precedent,”

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: Pharaoh's people became a precedent warning later people against following corrupt leaders instead of God's messengers.
rows.anchor: served as a precedent and an example for other people who chose to follow their corrupt leaders rather than messengers from God (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Makkan leaders likewise rejected Muhammad's prophethood by following corrupt leaders.
rows.anchor: as did the Makkan leaders in rejecting the prophethood of Muhammad.

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Q
rows.claim: On Judgment Day each community is gathered in ranks, kneeling before God for the Reckoning from shame.
rows.anchor: each religious community will be gathered in ranks (see 18:48c) with its members upon their knees for the Reckoning before God (Ṭ) due to the shame of that day (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: One reported view confines this kneeling fate to disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Some say that this fate is particular to the disbelievers (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another view applies the fate to believers and disbelievers as they await the Reckoning.
rows.anchor: others say it applies to believers and disbelievers alike when they are awaiting the Reckoning before God (Q).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another canonical reading says every community is called to its book while kneeling.
rows.anchor: According to another canonical reading, this verse could be rendered, “Thou wilt see every community upon its knees, every community called to its book” (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular “book” refers to each person's individual record, where angels record deeds at God's command.
rows.anchor: book is used in the singular to indicate the individual books in which each person’s deeds are recorded by the angels upon God’s Command

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the book with the Preserved Tablet containing God's commands and decrees.
rows.anchor: or the Preserved Tablet (85:22; Q), upon which all of God’s Commands and Decrees are said to have been written

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: One view holds that the address is spoken by the angels assigned to record human deeds.
rows.anchor: The address is spoken by the angels who were tasked with recording the deeds of human beings (R, Z)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another view holds that God speaks the address.
rows.anchor: The address is spoken by the angels who were tasked with recording the deeds of human beings (R, Z) or by God (Q).

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The book speaking against people means that it testifies to their deeds.
rows.anchor: That the book speaks against human beings means that it testifies to their deeds (Q, R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quran 18:49 depicts the record as exhaustive, omitting nothing and containing everything people did.
rows.anchor: It leaves out nothing, small or great, save that it has taken account thereof.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In light of the Prophet's saying that the Quran is a proof for or against a person, this verse may refer to the Quran.
rows.anchor: this verse could also be understood as a reference to the Quran.
